iOS 27 Beta 5 contains code related to a new feature that lets Apple verify the authenticity of iPhone photos.

The vast majority of iPhone users won't need this feature, which I'll explain shortly, but this move is just the beginning…

What is Apple Reference Image?

AI-generated images and videos are advancing rapidly, with a level of realism and detail that can be hard to distinguish from real photographs. This is being exploited by scammers and those deliberately spreading disinformation.

An industry organisation has been set up to address this, called the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA). It offers ways to identify genuine photographs and let viewers know whether a photo has been altered, with or without AI tools.

Over 500 companies have signed up to the C2PA scheme, but Apple appears to be going its own way for now, introducing an Apple Reference Image (ARI) feature. Anyone who takes a photo with an ARI-enabled iPhone can upload it to Apple's servers to verify its authenticity.

Why is this just the beginning?

Resources found in the latest beta show that the ARI feature will be off by default, as most iPhone users simply don't need it. It's aimed at journalists and those involved in legal proceedings who may need to provide independent evidence that their photos are genuine.

The initial applications of ARI may be limited, but as the use of AI-generated imagery becomes more widespread, features like this will become increasingly common. For example, the EU has recently published a code of practice regarding transparency around AI-generated content, designed to let people easily tell whether something is fake. It covers both images and text (see below).

This is voluntary for now, but several AI giants have expressed support. Anthropic says that all future Claude models will add digital watermarks to text and images. Notably, the company will implement this globally, not just in EU countries—which essentially means they expect this kind of requirement to become mandatory worldwide very soon.

How do you verify text is real?

The most eye-catching requirement in the EU plan is that AI firms must add digital watermarks to text outputs—not just images.

This can be done with invisible characters, like the ones I just used to replace the spaces between the words 'invisible' and 'characters'. This method resists copy and paste, though it's easily defeated with optical character recognition (OCR). For example, I have a tool on my Mac that handles this as easily as a screenshot (I installed it because some companies like to post statements as images on social media, which is frankly annoying).

It's been suggested that Anthropic may go further and use specific language patterns in Claude's outputs that can be detected even after the text has been put through OCR. I have plenty of thoughts on this, but it's beyond the scope of this piece.

If requirements like this do end up becoming mandatory, Apple will need to apply them to tools like Siri AI rewriting.

What do you think about this trend? Feel free to share in the comments.
